titre: Wegener Was Right, Fifty Years Too Early
accroche: In 1912, a meteorologist proposes that the continents drift. Geology judges it inadmissible, and will for half a century.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 6, 1912, a young German meteorologist, Alfred Wegener, presents to the Geologische Vereinigung in Frankfurt an idea that will occupy geology for fifty years: the continents are not fixed, they drift. The book that develops the thesis, *Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane* (“The Origin of Continents and Oceans”), appears in 1915.

## A good argument, a bad mechanism

Wegener relies on a body of evidence that is now classic: the resemblance of the Atlantic coastlines (Africa and South America nearly fit together), the continuity of rock formations and fossils on either side of the ocean, and similar glacial traces on continents now very far apart. His explanation gathers into a single story what regional geology had until then treated as separate coincidences.

But Wegener cannot answer the question put to him at once: what force would move entire continental masses? He points to the centrifugal force of the Earth's rotation and to lunar attraction, mechanisms that the physicists of the day calculate, rightly, to be far too weak. Lacking a credible engine, the community rejects the thesis wholesale.

## The organized rejection

In 1926, a symposium of the American Association of Petroleum Geologists concludes that the case for continental drift is closed, against it. The argument that keeps coming back: Wegener is not a geologist by training, and his mechanism is judged physically untenable. For the following decades, continental drift remains a marginal position, especially in North America.

## The missing proof

What Wegener lacked came from the ocean floor. In 1962, the geologist Harry Hess publishes *History of Ocean Basins*, in which he proposes that the ocean floors spread apart at the mid-ocean ridges, pushed by upwelling material from the mantle, a real engine, this time. The following year, Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews publish the decisive proof in *Nature*: the ocean floor carries symmetrical stripes of reversed magnetization on either side of the ridges, a frozen record of the spreading over time. Continental drift becomes plate tectonics, and wins acceptance within a few years.

## What the story shifts

Wegener dies in November 1930 on an expedition to Greenland, thirty years before the definitive proof. He was never wrong on the substance; he simply lacked the right mechanism, and the right tools to observe it. The episode remains a textbook case in the history of science: a correct idea can be rejected, rightly, for a time, as long as it comes with no verifiable mechanism, and accepted later on the strength of entirely different evidence from what was put forward at first.

repere.texte: Wegener presents his thesis on January 6, 1912, and develops it in a book published in 1915. In 1926, a symposium of the American Association of Petroleum Geologists judges the case for continental drift closed, against it. It takes until 1962 (Harry Hess) and then 1963 (Vine and Matthews, Nature) for a mechanism and direct proof to win acceptance.
repere.source: The Geological Society (London); Earth Sciences History, 1995

carte.punch: Wegener was right about the continents, fifty years before the proof.
carte.idee: In 1912, Wegener proposes that the continents drift. Lacking a credible mechanism, the community rejects the idea; a 1926 symposium judges it closed. It takes 1962 and seafloor spreading, then the magnetic stripes discovered in 1963, for the proof to win acceptance.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Biography, publication dates, and the circumstances of his death in Greenland in 1930.

quiz.question: Why was Wegener's thesis rejected by the geology of his day?
choix: Because the fossils he cited on either side of the Atlantic turned out to be fake
Because the coasts of Africa and South America do not in fact fit together
Because he offered no credible physical mechanism to explain the movement of the continents
Because no geological data then linked the two continents
quiz.explication: Wegener had a solid body of evidence (fossils, rock formations, glacial traces), but no known force could explain the movement of entire continental masses. That engine, seafloor spreading, was not demonstrated until 1962-1963, with the work of Hess and then of Vine and Matthews.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What evidence does Wegener put forward in 1912 to support the idea that the continents drift?
choix: Direct measurements of the continents' speed of movement, taken by triangulation
The resemblance of the Atlantic coastlines and the continuity of rock formations, fossils, and glacial traces
Seismic data showing active faults beneath the Atlantic Ocean
Accounts from sailors who had observed a growing gap between Europe and America
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wegener relies on the fit of the Atlantic coastlines, the continuity of rock formations and fossils on either side of the ocean, and similar glacial traces on distant continents.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the symposium of the American Association of Petroleum Geologists conclude in 1926?
choix: That continental drift must be tested by new expeditions before any judgment
That Wegener is right in substance, but that field data are still missing
That the debate must be settled by a vote of the members of the German geological society
That the case for continental drift is closed, Wegener's thesis rejected
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1926, a symposium of the American Association of Petroleum Geologists judges the case for continental drift closed, against Wegener's thesis, notably for lack of a credible mechanism.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What 1962 discovery finally provides a credible physical mechanism to explain the movement of the continents?
choix: Seafloor spreading through upwelling mantle material, proposed by Harry Hess
The detection of reversed magnetic fields in continental crust, by Wegener himself
Direct satellite measurement of the annual separation between Europe and America
The discovery of new identical fossils in Africa and South America
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1962, Harry Hess proposes in History of Ocean Basins that the ocean floors spread apart at the ridges, pushed by upwelling mantle material, an engine at last credible.
